en.title: Unreal Engine 6 Ditches Blueprints for AI-Powered Verse Coding
en.summary: Epic Games is set to radically alter Unreal Engine's development landscape by removing the long-standing Blueprints visual scripting system in favor of an AI-driven Verse programming language for Unreal Engine 6. This significant shift aims to streamline workflows but raises questions for developers accustomed to the current engine.
en.body:
Epic Games has announced a seismic shift for **Unreal Engine 6**, revealing that the engine will not launch with its widely adopted **Blueprints** visual scripting system. This decision, detailed by Epic Games executive vice president of development, Marcus Wassmer, signifies a move away from the familiar node-based system that has empowered countless developers for years. Instead, gameplay programming will primarily be handled by the **Verse** programming language, augmented by AI tools designed to assist in the transition from **Unreal Engine 5**.

Wassmer cited the declining cost of AI task completion and the successful AI-assisted conversion of **Fortnite**'s extensive Blueprint library to Verse as key drivers for this strategic pivot. While **Blueprints** have been a cornerstone for many, allowing artists and designers to implement complex logic without deep C++ knowledge, Epic appears confident that AI will bridge the gap. The company maintains that projects will still be convertible from UE5 to UE6, with AI playing a crucial role in this migration process. Details on the specific AI features and conversion tools for UE6 have not yet been fully elaborated upon, but the industry trend suggests a significant integration of AI into the engine's toolchain.

## The End of an Era for Visual Scripting?

This announcement has naturally sparked considerable discussion within the game development community. **Blueprints** have long been lauded as an accessible entry point into game development, serving as a powerful intermediate step between artistic intent and technical implementation. As former Valve developer Chet Faliszek noted, these systems create a "new skill in the middle there, between normal and expert." The prospect of losing this familiar and powerful toolset, forcing developers to either master **Verse** or rely heavily on AI prompting, presents a significant learning curve. For indie developers and those who have built entire projects, like the RPG **Queen's Domain**, using **Blueprints**, this change represents a fundamental alteration to their established workflows and a potential re-evaluation of their technical skill sets. The reliance on AI for core scripting functions also brings forth discussions about the determinism and control developers have over their creations.

## What's Next

Epic Games has not provided a definitive timeline for the full implementation of these changes in **Unreal Engine 6**. Developers are encouraged to stay tuned for further announcements regarding the specific AI tooling, **Verse** language advancements, and migration strategies that will be available. The industry will be watching closely to see how this bold departure from traditional scripting impacts the future of game development.

content_raw: Unreal Engine 6 will not launch with the engine's long-standard Blueprints scripting system. The news came in a Friday, November 19 post on the Unreal Engine website , written by Epic Games executive vice president of development, Marcus Wassmer. Here's Wassmer's top-level summary from the post: Blueprints have not (and it appears, will not) be deprecated in Unreal Engine 5, and the company maintains that projects will still be easy to convert from UE5 to UE6. Wassmer cited a declining cost in AI task completion as one reason for this belief, as well as the team's ongoing, but apparently successful conversion of Fortnite's Blueprint library to UE6's Verse programming language through an AI-assisted process. Blueprints are a widely-used feature of Unreal. Former Valve developer Chet Faliszek, an AI skeptic, has put out a vlog on the subject . Essentially, Faliszek argues that Blueprints (and features like them in other game engines) represent a middle ground between artistic and technical work, an introduction and skill builder for less technically-minded developers. Without them, such developers seemingly have to either learn Verse code, or integrate LLM prompting into their workflows. "We made a new skill in the middle there, between normal and expert," Faliszek said of intermediate tools like Blueprints. "To lose that determinism from game design, and instead have to prompt AI⁠—or write your own Verse … It's losing those tools that made all those designers and all those artists so powerful, to be able to do really powerful things and have access to really deep-down things, but in a safe way that the engineers can decide what that meant to them." A dark horse game of the year candidate, the first-person RPG Queen's Domain , was made with Unreal Engine. I recently spoke to co-developer Eric Berger, who specialized in art and design alongside the more technically-focused Bradley Boothe, a relationship that rhymes with the ones Faliszek outlined in his video. I spoke to Berger before seeing Epic's latest press release, but Berger already indicated that Unreal's AI pivot is prompting Freshly Baked Games to switch engines for its next project. I followed up with Berger about this Blueprint news, and the developer said that Blueprints were a major part of the workflow on Queen's Domain. I'm a layman in game development, but I think Wassmer's post elides that there is a large qualitative difference between doing any work via LLM prompt versus the old-fashioned way⁠—I don't like or want to use these tools, myself, and I don't think that's an unpopular stance. Commenter ZILtoid1991 on Faliszek's video compared the move to Apple removing headphone jacks on the iPhone, a comparison I find fruitful. It was hugely unpopular at the time, and is still derided by enthusiasts, but it also worked .
